slides.1.title: Douro — History, Geography and Sub-regions
slides.1.html:
The Douro is Portugal's most historically significant region; in 1756 it became the world's first wine region under continuous government regulation.

🗺️ Three Sub-regions

  • Baixo Corgo (Lower Corgo): closest to the sea with relatively more rain; fresh, lively reds, often used as the base for Port
  • Cima Corgo (Upper Corgo): a more continental climate and the core of the finest Ports (such as Vintage Port)
  • Douro Superior (Upper Douro): the most inland, with an extreme continental climate, the hottest and driest summers and the highest degree of modern mechanisation

📊 Key Figures

  • About 50% of the wine goes into Porto (Port)
  • The other 50% becomes high-quality unfortified reds and whites under Douro DOC
  • The Vinho Regional "Duriense" overlaps with the Douro area
slides.2.title: Porto (Port) — What Is a Fortified Wine?
slides.2.html:
Port is Portugal's most famous wine. During production, grape spirit (Aguardente) is added to halt fermentation and preserve natural sweetness.

🔬 The Fortification Process

  • When fermentation reaches about 7-8% alcohol, 77% grape spirit is added
  • The spirit kills the yeast, fermentation stops and a large amount of residual sugar is retained
  • Final alcohol: 19–22% vol.
  • Traditionally, Lagares (stone troughs) are used for foot treading to extract colour

🍷 Main Types (Introduction)

  • Ruby: young, deep red, fruity
  • Tawny: oxidative ageing in oak casks, golden-brown, with nutty and toffee aromas
  • Vintage: the top declared vintages, able to age 20-50 years
  • LBV (Late Bottled Vintage): a secondary vintage style, good value

slides.4.title: ⏳ Port Ageing: Reductive Ruby vs. Oxidative Tawny
slides.4.description: An interactive look at the difference between Ruby Port's reductive ageing (in bottle and large vats, preserving deep colour and fruit) and Tawny Port's oxidative ageing (long contact with oxygen in small pipes, developing complex dried-fruit, nut and coffee aromas). Includes the actual average ages behind 10/20/30/40 Year Tawny and key tips for choosing.
slides.5.question: What alcohol range is Porto (Port) usually in?
slides.5.explanation: Port reaches 19–22% alcohol through fortification (the addition of grape spirit) while retaining a large amount of residual sugar, creating a distinctive sweet fortified wine.
slides.6.question: In the "port-styles" pyramid, which of the following Ports is aged reductively in bottle (retaining deep colour and fresh fruit) rather than oxidatively in oak casks?
slides.6.explanation: Vintage Port spends only about 2 years in large vats (the regulatory limit is about 2.5 years) before bottling, then ages in bottle for a long time (50+ years), a reductive style that keeps deep colour and fresh fruit. Tawnies (10/20/40 Year, Colheita) are all oxidatively aged through long contact with oxygen in small pipes, giving a red-brown colour with dried-fruit and coffee notes.
slides.7.question: In the "port-aging" supplementary lesson, what does the "20" mean on a bottle labelled "20 Years Tawny"?
slides.7.options.0: The youngest wine in the blend is at least 20 years old
slides.7.options.1: All the wines in the blend are of a 20-year-old vintage
slides.7.options.2: The blend has an average style age of about 20 years
slides.7.options.3: It must age at least 20 years after bottling
slides.7.explanation: The age in "10/20/30/40 Years Tawny" is not a release date; it indicates that the wine tastes and is styled like a blend of that average age. The master blender combines many casks of different ages so that the finished wine matches the "20 Years" style. In practice the blend contains wines ranging from 5 to 40 years.
